title: Interspecies clock comparison below $5 \times 10^{-18}$ uncertainty with a transportable clock
authors: Chetan Vishwakarma, Ingo Nosske, Tim Lücke, Martin Steinel, Melina Filzinger, Erik Benkler, Sören Dörscher, Nils Huntemann, Christian Lisdat
abstract: We report a measurement of the optical frequency ratio between the $^2\mathrm{S}_{1/2}(F=0)$--${^2\mathrm{F}_{7/2}(F=3)}$ electric-octupole (E3) transition of $^{171}$Yb$^{+}$ and the $^1\mathrm{S}_0$--${^3\mathrm{P}_0}$ transition of $^{87}$Sr, $ν_{\mathrm{Yb}^{+}}/ν_\mathrm{Sr} = 1.495\,991\,618\,544\,900\,588\,1(65)$. Reaching a fractional uncertainty of $4.3 \times 10^{-18}$, this result improves upon the previous best by more than a factor of three and is among the few that meet the requirements for interspecies clock comparisons specified by the roadmap towards the redefinition of the SI second. The comparison is between a transportable optical lattice clock and a stationary single-ion clock. It spans a period of nearly two years, during which the transportable clock was intermittently operated off-campus. The ratio was reproducibly measured during four separate campaigns, which are consistent within their statistical uncertainties. The results demonstrate reproducible $10^{-18}$ level operation of the transportable clock and thus validate its application for chronometric geodesy and as a transfer standard for inter-institute clock comparisons, e.g., in the absence of optical fiber links.
summary: The authors report a highly precise comparison of the optical frequencies between an ytterbium single-ion clock and a strontium lattice clock, achieving an uncertainty below $5 	imes 10^{-18}$. This result significantly advances the field by demonstrating the reliable operation of transportable atomic clocks for fundamental physical measurements. It provides crucial data supporting the roadmap for redefining the SI second.
main_problem: The primary goal is achieving ultra-high accuracy interspecies clock comparisons, particularly involving a transportable clock, to meet requirements for redefining the SI second.
main_result:

u_{	ext{Yb}^+}/
u_{	ext{Sr}}$, significantly improving previous records and validating the use of transportable clocks for fundamental measurements.
method: The experiment measured the optical frequency ratio between a stationary single-ion clock ($^{171}	ext{Yb}^+$) and a transportable lattice clock ($^{87}	ext{Sr}$) over multiple campaigns, using an ultrastable laser as a common reference.
model_or_system: The system involves comparing the electric-octupole (E3) transition of $^{171}	ext{Yb}^+$ with the $^1	ext{S}_0$--${^3	ext{P}_0}$ transition of $^{87}	ext{Sr}$. The methodology requires precise control over clock laser frequencies and accounting for environmental effects like relativistic redshift.

important_parameters: Fractional uncertainty of $4.3 	imes 10^{-18}$; the comparison spans nearly two years across four separate campaigns.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that systematic errors, such as those related to lattice light shifts or gravitational potential variations, can be accurately modeled and corrected for.

paper_structure: The paper details the experimental setup comparing two different atomic species' optical transitions, presents data collected across multiple time periods/campaigns, analyzes the resulting frequency ratios to determine a weighted average value, and discusses the implications for SI second redefinition.
why_interesting: This work represents state-of-the-art precision measurement in quantum metrology. The ability to compare clocks using transportable standards is critical for extending fundamental physics tests beyond fixed laboratory settings.
